jq 1.8 negates a literal to a literal (jqlang/jq#3242, fixing jqlang/jq#2704), so `-1e1000` prints `-1E+1000`; jq 1.7.1 negates to the double `-1.7976931348623157e+308`. succinctly follows 1.8.2 (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, #7453).

`"11:30 PM" | strptime("%I:%M %p")`: the weekday (element 6) is 6 in jq 1.7.1 on macOS and 0 in succinctly. It is the platform libc's weekday and yearday of a format that sets no date (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, "`strptime` weekday and yearday of a format that sets no date", #5340, #5383): jq's macOS build derives it from the unset date (`1900-01-00`) with its own `set_tm_wday()`, glibc leaves jq's `8`/`367` sentinels, and succinctly answers the date's own weekday. `"12"|strptime("%H")` and `"3"|strptime("%d")` differ the same way.

Same platform-dependent weekday as `locale-strptime-ampm-c`, under `de_DE.UTF-8`, on a host without that locale (it falls back to `C`). A host that has the locale matches: neither tool parses `PM` there, and both exit 5.
Same platform-dependent weekday as `locale-strptime-ampm-c`, under `en_US.UTF-8`.

Same platform-dependent weekday as `locale-strptime-ampm-c`, under `tr_TR.UTF-8`, on a host without that locale (it falls back to `C`). A host that has the locale matches: neither tool parses `PM` there, and both exit 5.

`"Thursday, March 05 2015" | strptime("%A, %B %d %Y")` under `de_DE.UTF-8`: glibc's `strptime` reads the `C` locale's English names as well as the locale's own, so a glibc jq 1.7.1 answers where the macOS pin's libc and succinctly exit 5 (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, "glibc `jq` under a locale, measured"). Only a Linux host that has `de_DE` shows it: without the locale both tools fall back to `C` and agree.

`"Thursday, March 05 2015" | strptime("%A, %B %d %Y")` under `tr_TR.UTF-8`: the same glibc behaviour as `locale-strptime-en-de-de`, reading the `C` locale's English names beside the locale's own. Only a Linux host that has `tr_TR` shows it.

`--stream -s` over input with no trailing newline keeps the last closing event in the array in jq 1.8.2 (jqlang/jq#3279, a fix of the 1.7.1 slurp loop); jq 1.7.1 prints the array and then the held closing event as a second output (`[1,2]` gives `[[[0],1],[[1],2]]` then `[[1]]`). succinctly follows 1.8.2 (#7523), and for the fault at the end of the text too (#7807): `2[` under `--stream-errors -s` is `[[[],2],["Unfinished JSON term at EOF at line 1, column 2",[0]]]`, where jq 1.7.1 prints `[[[],2]]` and then the fault event as a second output. `[-5,0,1,0,0,0,0,0] | strftime("%y|%C|%D")` is `05|-0|01/01/05` in jq 1.7.1 on macOS (the libc's `_yconv`: the remainder's absolute value, and `-0` for a century of 0) and succinctly follows it. A glibc jq prints `95|-1|01/01/95` (the floored remainder and quotient), as it prints `%Y` of year -5 as `-5` where the pin prints `-005` (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, "negative years"). `foreach (try (.[:2])) as $x0 ((. , .); (.[-1:]))` on an object: its INIT is a generator, and jq 1.7.1 runs the SOURCE of the second INIT output on `null` (`null | .[:2]` is `null`), so the update `.[-1:]` slices the object and fails with `Cannot index object with object` (exit 5). jq 1.8 runs the SOURCE on the real input for every INIT output (jqlang/jq#3266, a bug fix), where `.[:2]` on an object fails inside `try`, so jq 1.8.2 and succinctly print nothing (exit 0). The syntax:foreach-gen-init entry is the same difference (#7519).

`. | last((. | nulls))` on an array: `nulls` yields nothing, and jq 1.7.1's `last(f)` (`reduce f as $x (null; $x)`) answers its `null` seed, where jq 1.8 yields nothing (jqlang/jq#3179, a bug fix); jq 1.8.2 and succinctly print nothing (exit 0). The syntax:man-last-empty entry is the same difference (#7518).

Under `ulimit -v` 64 MiB, 1M-integer array: the reference jq 1.7.1 aborts; succinctly answers, on an evaluation stack sized to the cap (#5634).

Under `ulimit -v` 64 MiB a 20 MB string is read by jq but aborts succinctly on a failed allocation. A trivial run already maps about 42 MiB (the binary, the main thread's 8 MiB stack and the evaluation stack, 16 MiB at the least under a cap, #5634), and the document takes 28 MiB more: the input, and its index in two allocations of 2.5 MB and 5 MB. That is the semi-index kept whole beside the input, not a leak: it fits in 70 MiB on Linux aarch64. How the run fails under the cap depends on how much memory the build maps, and a run records either class: a build that maps a little more stops at the read of the input and exits 2 with `jq: error: out of memory`, and one that maps less gets past that read to an index allocation that is not guarded and aborts (`memory allocation of N bytes failed`, killed by a signal). jq answers in both cases, so the entry stands for either.

Under `ulimit -v` 64 MiB, 300000-key object: the reference jq 1.7.1 aborts on x86_64 Linux; succinctly answers, on an evaluation stack sized to the cap (#5634). Whether jq aborts depends on the host's address-space footprint, not its architecture: the object needs most of the 64 MiB, so jq answers on Linux aarch64 (Neoverse-V2) yet aborts there too under a slightly lower cap (about 60000 KiB, measured with Ubuntu 24.04's jq 1.7). The entry is volatile so that a host where jq fits is not called stale (#7009).

`[range(1e8)] | length` under `ulimit -v` 512 MiB: jq 1.7.1 and succinctly both abort (killed by a signal, no exit status). Rust ends the process on a failed allocation (`memory allocation of N bytes failed`) where jq's `jv_mem_alloc` prints `cannot allocate memory` and aborts, so the output matches; a graceful error would need every container growth to be fallible.
`"a" * 1e9` under `ulimit -v` 512 MiB: jq 1.7.1 aborts; succinctly exits 5 with a graceful error.

jq 1.8 negates a literal to a literal (jqlang/jq#3242, fixing jqlang/jq#2704), so `-1e1000 | tojson` is `"-1E+1000"`; jq 1.7.1 answers `"-1.7976931348623157e+308"`. succinctly follows 1.8.2 (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, #7453).

A user-defined function recursing 10000 deep: jq answers (about 3 s); succinctly's stack guard refuses with `exceeded maximum recursion depth` (ADR-0025). The refusal is not immediate, so whether it arrives inside the 10 s deadline depends on the host's speed, and a run records either class for succinctly: `error` (exit 5) where it does, as on an Apple M4 Pro, and `timeout` where it does not, as on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X under Linux (#7891).

Recursion 100000 deep: jq does not finish within 10 s; succinctly's stack guard refuses (ADR-0025). The refusal is not immediate, so whether it arrives inside the 10 s deadline depends on the host's speed, and a run records either class for succinctly: `error` (exit 5) where it does, as on an Apple M4 Pro, and `timeout` where it does not, as on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X under Linux (#7891).

Tail-position recursion 100000 deep: jq does not finish within 10 s; succinctly's stack guard refuses (ADR-0025), so it gets no tail-call elimination. The refusal is not immediate, so whether it arrives inside the 10 s deadline depends on the host's speed, and a run records either class for succinctly: `error` (exit 5) where it does, as on an Apple M4 Pro, and `timeout` where it does not, as on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X under Linux (#7891).
`gsub("a";"b")` over 100000 characters: jq 1.7.1 does not finish within 10 s; succinctly answers in tens of milliseconds.

`[match("a";"g")]` over 100000 characters: jq 1.7.1 does not finish within 10 s on an M4 Pro (5.7 s on a 7950X); succinctly answers in tens of milliseconds. Whether jq beats the deadline depends on the host (it timed out on an M4 Pro and on a GitHub-hosted x86_64 Linux runner, #5565).
add(f) is new in jq 1.8; succinctly follows the 1.7.1 pin (ADR-0018).
have_decnum is new in jq 1.8; succinctly follows the 1.7.1 pin (ADR-0018).
have_literal_numbers is new in jq 1.8; succinctly follows the 1.7.1 pin (ADR-0018).
trimstr(s) is new in jq 1.8; succinctly follows the 1.7.1 pin (ADR-0018).

A `foreach` whose INIT is a generator runs its SOURCE on the real input for every INIT output, as jq 1.8 does (jqlang/jq#3266, a bug fix); jq 1.7.1 runs it on `null` after the first output, so `.a[]` raises `Cannot iterate over null` (exit 5) where succinctly and jq 1.8.2 print `[2,4,7,3,5,8]`. `reduce` keeps the 1.7.1 behaviour, as 1.8.2 does.

A program's `-0` is the literal `0` in jq 1.8 (jqlang/jq#3242, fixing jqlang/jq#2704), so `1 / -0` names `number (0)` as the divisor; jq 1.7.1 names `number (-0)`. succinctly follows 1.8.2 (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, #7453).

`last(f)` of an `f` that yields nothing yields nothing in jq 1.8 (jqlang/jq#3179, a fix of the 1.7.1 `reduce f as $x (null; $x)` definition); jq 1.7.1 answers its `null` seed, so `[last(empty)]` is `[null]` there. succinctly follows 1.8.2 (#7518).

jq 1.8 negates a literal to a literal (jqlang/jq#3242, fixing jqlang/jq#2704) and a zero to positive zero, so `[-0, -0.0, 0e5]` is `[0,0.0,0E+5]`; jq 1.7.1 answers `[-0,-0,0E+5]`. succinctly follows 1.8.2 (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, #7453).

A program's `-0` is the literal `0` in jq 1.8, which negates a literal's decimal (jqlang/jq#3242, fixing jqlang/jq#2704), so it prints `0`; jq 1.7.1 negates to the double `-0`. succinctly follows 1.8.2 (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, #7453).

A program's `-0` is the literal `0` in jq 1.8, which negates a literal's decimal (jqlang/jq#3242, fixing jqlang/jq#2704), so `[1.0,1e1000,-0]|@json` is `"[1.0,1E+1000,0]"`; jq 1.7.1 negates to the double `-0`. succinctly follows 1.8.2 (docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md, #7453).
`@urid` is new in jq 1.8, which decodes it; jq 1.7.1 answers `urid is not a valid format` (exit 5). succinctly follows the 1.8 behaviour for this format, documented in CLAUDE.md's format table.

jq 1.7.1's own test `fromjson | isnan` on `"nan1234"` expects `true`: a NaN with a payload is an invalid numeric literal in jq 1.8 (CVE-2024-53427, "Reject NaN with payload while parsing JSON"), which dropped this case from its jq.test. succinctly follows 1.8 (#7522, docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md) and raises `Invalid numeric literal`, as jq 1.8.2 does.

jq 1.7.1's own test `[match("( )*"; "g")]` on `"abc"` expects each empty match's capture to be `{"offset":0,"string":"",...}` (the match's offset). jq 1.8 reports an optional group that takes no part in an empty match as unmatched (jqlang/jq#3238, a bug fix), `{"offset":-1,"string":null,"length":0,"name":null}`, and its own onig.test expects that; succinctly follows 1.8 (#7520, docs/compliance/jq/limitations.md).
